bookTitle: Technical Analysis of the Financial Markets (John J. Murphy)

facts.statement: A futures contract is an exchange-traded, standardized agreement to buy or sell an underlying asset for a specific price at a specified future date.

sourceCitation.book: Technical Analysis of the Financial Markets (John J. Murphy)
sourceCitation.excerpt: Futures Contract: An exchange-traded, standardized agreement to buy or sell an underlying asset for a specific price at a specified future date

facts.statement: A long position is an agreement to purchase the underlying asset, whereas a short position is an agreement to sell the underlying asset.

sourceCitation.book: Technical Analysis of the Financial Markets (John J. Murphy)
sourceCitation.excerpt: Long Position: The agreement to buy the underlying asset. Short Position: The agreement to sell the underlying asset.

facts.topic: Daily Price Limits and Position Limits
facts.statement: Exchanges set daily price limits—consisting of limit up and limit down thresholds—to curb speculative volatility, alongside position limits restricting the maximum number of contracts a speculator can hold.

sourceCitation.book: Technical Analysis of the Financial Markets (John J. Murphy)
sourceCitation.excerpt: Daily Price Limits: Limits set by exchanges to curb speculative volatility; includes limit up (maximum upward movement) and limit down (maximum downward movement)

facts.topic: Convergence of Futures Price to Spot Price
facts.statement: As the delivery period approaches, the futures price converges toward the spot price (F_T ≈ S_T) through arbitrage and demand mechanisms.

sourceCitation.book: Technical Analysis of the Financial Markets (John J. Murphy)
sourceCitation.excerpt: As the delivery period approaches, the futures price converges to the spot price (F_T ≈ S_T)

facts.statement: The gain or loss on a long futures position equals contract size multiplied by exit price minus entry price, while a short position gain or loss equals contract size multiplied by entry price minus exit price.

sourceCitation.book: Technical Analysis of the Financial Markets (John J. Murphy)
sourceCitation.excerpt: Gain/Loss (Long) = Contract Size × (Futures Price_Exit - Futures Price_Entry)

facts.topic: Grade Price Adjustment for CME Corn
facts.statement: For CME Corn futures, No. 1 Yellow corn commands a 1.5 cents per bushel premium over the futures settlement price, whereas No. 3 Yellow corn carries a 1.5 cents per bushel discount.

sourceCitation.book: Technical Analysis of the Financial Markets (John J. Murphy)
sourceCitation.excerpt: Settlement Price_No. 1 Yellow = Futures Price + 1.5 cents/bushel

variables.definition: Standard settlement futures price (for No. 2 Yellow corn)

facts.topic: Unanticipated Delivery of Live Cattle Contracts
facts.statement: An inexperienced employee accidentally bought one additional CME live cattle contract instead of selling to close, resulting in an open long position of 2 contracts (80,000 lbs of cattle) requiring physical delivery 2,000 miles away and one week of animal care.

sourceCitation.book: Technical Analysis of the Financial Markets (John J. Murphy)
sourceCitation.excerpt: Trading ceased, leaving the financial institution holding a long position in 2 live cattle futures contracts (80,000 lbs of cattle)

numericalDetails.context: Accidental long position expiration leading to forced physical acceptance and care of live cattle until the next auction.

facts.topic: CME Treasury Bond and Note Specifications
facts.statement: CME Treasury bond futures specify a face value of $100,000 with underlying maturities between 15 and 25 years on the first day of the delivery month, while 10-Year Treasury note futures cover maturities between 6.5 and 10 years.

sourceCitation.book: Technical Analysis of the Financial Markets (John J. Murphy)
sourceCitation.excerpt: Underlying asset = U.S. Treasury bond with maturity between 15 and 25 years on 1st day of delivery month; Face value = $100,000

numericalDetails.context: Contract delivery asset specifications for CME Treasury futures.

facts.topic: ICE FCOJ and CME Mini Nasdaq Contract Sizes
facts.statement: ICE Frozen Concentrate Orange Juice requires U.S. Grade A with Brix value of at least 62.5 degrees, while CME Mini Nasdaq 100 contracts have a multiplier of 20 times the index versus 100 times for the regular contract.

sourceCitation.book: Technical Analysis of the Financial Markets (John J. Murphy)
sourceCitation.excerpt: Brix value ≥ 62.5°; Size = 20 times the Nasdaq 100 index (compared to 100 times for the regular contract)

numericalDetails.context: Standardization parameters for FCOJ quality and Mini Nasdaq contract sizing.

facts.topic: The Delivery Mechanism as a Price Anchor
facts.statement: Although physical delivery takes place in less than 1% of futures transactions, the potential for delivery acts as the essential anchor tying the futures price to the spot price at expiration.

sourceCitation.book: Technical Analysis of the Financial Markets (John J. Murphy)
sourceCitation.excerpt: physical delivery occurs in less than 1% of trades, the possibility of final delivery is the essential anchor that ties the futures price to the spot price at maturity

generalAssumptions: Physical delivery is inconvenient and costly, leading market participants to close out the vast majority of positions prior to delivery.
Arbitrageurs will exploit price discrepancies whenever futures prices deviate from spot prices during the delivery period, forcing convergence.
Contract standardization ensures complete fungibility across positions traded on the same exchange.
